title: Backend CORS reflects arbitrary Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
description: The Express.js backend reflects any Origin header value in Access-Control-Allow-Origin while also setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This allows any attacker-controlled page to make credentialed cross-origin requests and read the full response, effectively bypassing the same-origin policy for authenticated sessions.
evidence_safe: OPTIONS /auth/me with Origin:https://attacker.com returns 204 with access-control-allow-origin:https://attacker.com + access-control-allow-credentials:true
evidence_quarantined: HTTP/2 204 | access-control-allow-origin: https://attacker.com | access-control-allow-credentials: true | access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE,OPTIONS

title: No OIDC nonce validation found in NextAuth.js Azure AD configuration bundles
description: Analysis of all 22 JS bundles reveals no nonce generation or validation patterns in the OIDC/OAuth2 flow. All nonce references in bundles are React CSP script nonces, not OIDC nonce parameters. Without nonce validation, id_token replay attacks against the callback endpoint may be feasible if an attacker can obtain a valid id_token.
evidence_safe: Zero OIDC nonce generation/validation patterns found across 1MB of concatenated JS bundles; all nonce refs are React/Next.js CSP nonces

title: CSRF token cookie is non-HttpOnly, readable by JavaScript (double-submit pattern)
description: The application uses a double-submit cookie pattern where the csrf-token cookie is intentionally readable by JavaScript. The backendFetch helper reads it via document.cookie and forwards it as x-csrf-token header. While this is the intended design, any XSS vulnerability provides full CSRF bypass capability because the attacker's JavaScript can read the CSRF token directly.
evidence_safe: document.cookie.match(/csrf-token=([^;]+)/) used in backendFetch; token forwarded as x-csrf-token header to all backend API calls

title: Client-side RBAC enforcement via usePermissions() hook — server enforcement unverifiable from bundles
description: The application uses a usePermissions() React hook backed by /rbac/me/permissions to gate UI elements. Permissions are stored client-side in a Set and checked with d.has(permissionKey). While permissions are fetched from the backend, the rendering logic is purely client-side. If any backend endpoint does not independently re-validate permissions, UI manipulation or direct API calls could bypass role-based access controls.
evidence_safe: usePermissions() returns hasPermission fn from effectivePermissions Set loaded from /rbac/me/permissions; UI rendering conditioned on this client-side Set

title: Git commit SHA and backend URL hardcoded in production JavaScript bundle
description: The production bundle embeds the full git commit hash (61c5fdeac36ed85a883ae93b78c06d03f9f4e4a1) in Datadog telemetry configuration and hardcodes the backend Azure Container Apps URL. This reveals exact source code version for vulnerability correlation and confirms infrastructure topology. The NEXT_PUBLIC_BACKEND_URL validation error message also discloses the full backend URL.
evidence_safe: version:61c5fdeac36ed85a883ae93b78c06d03f9f4e4a1 in Datadog config; backend URL hardcoded as https://revops-dev.livelystone-c1480484.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io

title: x-powered-by: Express header discloses backend framework
description: The backend returns an x-powered-by: Express header on all responses including error responses. This confirms the backend framework and enables targeted framework-specific attack enumeration.
evidence_safe: HTTP response header x-powered-by: Express present on all backend responses

title: User ID interpolated directly into RBAC API path without server-side ownership validation observable
description: Multiple backend API paths interpolate user-controlled IDs directly into endpoint paths including /rbac/users/${e}/role, /rbac/users/${e}/permissions, and /users/${e}/access. If the backend does not validate that the requesting user owns or has rights over the target ID, horizontal privilege escalation (IDOR) is possible by substituting another user's ID.
evidence_safe: Template literal paths: /rbac/users/${e}/role, /rbac/users/${e}/permissions, /users/${e}/access with no client-side ownership check before call

title: CORS wildcard origin reflection with credentials enabled on all backend routes
description: The Express backend reflects any arbitrary Origin header value verbatim in Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Tested across /auth/me, /rbac/roles, /users, /health, /auth/token — all reflect attacker-controlled origins. Null origin is also reflected, enabling sandboxed iframe attacks.

access-control-allow-credentials: true
access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE,OPTIONS

The response includes PostgreSQL exact version with build hash, OS architecture (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu), GCC compiler version, and deployment environment names. This information aids in targeted exploitation.

title: Express backend route surface enumerated — 50+ routes discovered behind global auth middleware

Routes span: auth, users, admin, rbac, accounts, contacts, deals, pipelines, graphql, docs/swagger, webhooks, integrations, audit, billing, and internal paths. All paths are protected by a global auth middleware returning consistent 401 JSON error.

title: CORS Wildcard Origin Reflection with Credentials — Backend Accepts Any Origin
description: The backend Express API reflects any supplied Origin header in Access-Control-Allow-Origin while simultaneously setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This was confirmed by the nuclei cors-misconfig template (arbitrary-origin match) and by manual curl tests with evil.attacker.com, null, and attacker.com origins. CORS headers are returned even on 401 unauthenticated responses, meaning an attacker-controlled page can read any cross-origin response from an authenticated user's session.
evidence_safe: Nuclei cors-misconfig template confirmed: [cors-misconfig:arbitrary-origin] [http] [info] https://revops-dev.livelystone-c1480484.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io [cors_origin='https://revops-dev.livelystone-c1480484.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io.*.e7szh.com']. Manual curl confirmed: Origin: https://evil.attacker.com -> access-control-allow-origin: https://evil.attacker.com + access-control-allow-credentials: true on HTTP/2 200.

title: CORS Null Origin Accepted with Credentials — Sandbox/Iframe Exploitation Path
description: The backend accepts Origin: null with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This enables exploitation via iframe sandbox (sandbox attribute creates null-origin context) or via data: URI attacks. An attacker hosting a sandboxed iframe can make credentialed requests to the backend and read responses, bypassing same-origin policy.
evidence_safe: curl -H 'Origin: null' -H 'Cookie: test=1' https://revops-dev.livelystone-c1480484.westus2.azurecontainerapps.io/health -> HTTP/2 200, access-control-allow-credentials: true, access-control-allow-origin: null

title: CORS OPTIONS Preflight Accepts Arbitrary Origin — Credentialed POST Requests Enabled
description: The backend returns HTTP 204 to OPTIONS preflight requests from arbitrary origins with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and Access-Control-Allow-Headers including Authorization. This means browsers will allow credentialed cross-origin POST/PUT/DELETE requests with custom headers to all API endpoints, not just GET requests.
evidence_safe: curl -X OPTIONS -H 'Origin: https://attacker.com' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization,Content-Type' /api/users -> HTTP/2 204, access-control-allow-origin: https://attacker.com, access-control-allow-credentials: true, access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE,OPTIONS

title: Missing Content-Security-Policy on Next.js Frontend — XSS Escalation Risk
description: The frontend at revops-dev.vercel.app does not set a Content-Security-Policy header. Combined with the absence of X-Frame-Options, this enables XSS attacks to escalate to full session compromise and enables clickjacking attacks on authentication flows.
evidence_safe: Nuclei http-missing-security-headers template confirmed: content-security-policy, x-frame-options, x-content-type-options, strict-transport-security, referrer-policy, permissions-policy, clear-site-data, cross-origin-embedder-policy, cross-origin-opener-policy, cross-origin-resource-policy, x-permitted-cross-domain-policies — all missing on https://revops-dev.vercel.app

title: Missing All Security Headers on Express Backend — 11 Headers Absent
description: The Express.js backend is missing all security response headers: CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COEP, COOP, CORP, Clear-Site-Data, and X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies. No Helmet.js or equivalent middleware is configured.
evidence_safe: Nuclei http-missing-security-headers confirmed 11 absent headers: content-security-policy, x-frame-options, x-content-type-options, strict-transport-security, referrer-policy, permissions-policy, clear-site-data, cross-origin-embedder-policy, cross-origin-opener-policy, cross-origin-resource-policy, x-permitted-cross-domain-policies on backend

title: Sensitive File Paths Return 401 (Not 404) — Route Enumeration via Status Code Differential
description: Sensitive paths (/.env, /.env.local, /package.json, /.git/config, /.git/HEAD, /server.js) return HTTP 401 instead of 404 on the backend. This confirms these route patterns are handled by the application, enabling attackers to infer the existence of configuration files and enumerate protected routes. Combined with the CORS misconfiguration, an attacker could potentially access these if authentication is bypassed.
evidence_safe: /.env -> HTTP 401, /.env.local -> HTTP 401, /package.json -> HTTP 401, /.git/config -> HTTP 401, /.git/HEAD -> HTTP 401, /server.js -> HTTP 401 on backend. Returns 401 not 404, confirming route existence.
